articles.text: Great preparations are being made at Bismarck for the meeting of the legislature, which will convene at the new capitol building January 1. The session will be short, sharp and decisive, as much work must be done. Several parts of the territory need special legislation, and will [doubtless?] get it. E. W. Martin, recently elected legislator, is urged especially by the Black Hills papers for speaker. Although Mr. Martin is a young man he could fill the position with credit. He seems to be the unanimous choice of the Black Hills delegation.
articles.summary: The legislature will meet at the new capitol in Bismarck January 1; E. W. Martin is urged by Black Hills papers for speaker.

articles.text: The notice for a meeting of the cattle men of this district, which we publish for the second time should attract the attention of every man on and in the neighborhood of the river who is interested in stock. The reasons are so manifest that an organization should be formed, that there is no need of enlarging on them. It is imperative above all things that the cattle men should be united to be successful in movements for their good. A number of points will come up for action at the meeting of December 19, and it is important that every cattle man in this district attend, as each should have a voice in the decisions. Should there be only a partial attendance or should the interest be half-hearted the effort to organize will be useless. Unanimous and united action will be of incalculable benefit to our stock men.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy urges every cattleman in the district to attend the December 19 stockmen's meeting and organize.

articles.headline: A Kick.
articles.text:
We have nothing but the kindliest feelings toward the N. P. Ex. Co., but we are nevertheless heartily glad that the Wells, Fargo Ex. Co. are making a beginning toward destroying a monopoly which is keeping this country down. The rates on everything are far higher than they are in the east. For this there is some reason, inasmuch as railroads, etc., cost much more to build. We are, however, laboring under the disadvantage, all over Dakota, of being a new country and paying higher prices for articles we use than almost any other part of the country.

Take the items of freight, express, passenger and telegraph rates that have come under our personal notice. A car load of freight from Milwaukee to St. Paul was thirty-four dollars. From St. Paul to Medora it was three hundred and sixty-four dollars. This was an unclassified lot of goods. Classified carloads have come nearer five hundred dollars. That these rates are extremely profitable is abundantly shown by the fac[t] that the N. P. is very well satisfied to ship goods to Medora for the Black Hills at fifty cents a hundred, unclassified, or one hundred and fifty dollars a car load. It is an actual fact, coming constantly under our notice since shipments began from Medora to the Hills, that freight from St. Paul, Chicago, and in fact all eastern points, is landed in Deadwood cheaper than the same freight can be landed in Medora for local consumption. It is also a fact, demonstrated by personal experience, that owing to this state of affairs, goods of almost every description are actually sold in the Hills cheaper than they can be sold in Medora. When we take into consideration the fact that the rail journey is equal, and that in addition the Hills goods must be loaded on wagons and freighted across country two hundred miles, it shows that there is "something rotten in Denmark." It shows that merely because it has the power, the Northern Pacific railroad is charging exhorbitant rates, and rates way above those it could adopt at a profit.

Almost exactly the same points can be brought against the express rates that have been mentioned in reference to freight. The Wells, Fargo Express Co., as is well known, do not by any means "stand in" as well as the N. P. Ex. Co., but they are, metaphorically, "knocking the eye out" of the N. P. on rates.

The passenger rates are also unreasonably high. Five, six, seven, eight, and in some cases we think ten cents a mile are charged. This is beyond all reason, and should be regulated immediately by the legislatures of the territories passed through. To show conclusively that these rates are not essential to the existence or profit of the road, we will mention the fact that it was, and probably is possible to buy a ticket from New York city to Portland, Oregon, cheaper than one from St. Paul to Missoula.

While we are about it, an illustration of telegraphic charges may not be inapt. Ten words from Medora to St. Paul, night rate, is sixty cents. Ten words to Grand Rapids, Michigan, is seventp-five cents. In this case the whole line is under the management of one concern, and the injustice of the discrimination is more apparent. It does not cost a particle more to conduct a telegraph line in this country than it does in the east, yet the same telegram costs only one-fourth more in going twice the distance, and has to be repeated twice. Oh, consistency, thy name is not a railroad or a telegraph monopoly.

The above illustrations show the difference between monopoly and competition. The time is probably far distant when just rates will be established and maintained, unless the Northern Pacific wakes up to the fact that their short-sighted policy of extortionate rates is the surest way in the world to cut their own throats.
articles.summary: Editorial attacking Northern Pacific freight, express, passenger and telegraph rates and welcoming Wells, Fargo express competition.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
To prevent bulls running on the range during the winter, for the benefit of cattle men, I have established and fitted up a bull ranch on the Little Missouri. I will receive, care for and feed hay to all bulls given in my charge for the sum of $2 per month per bull. The bull round-up started on Monday, November 18th, 1884, and all bulls will be received at the Royal Chambord ranch.

For further particulars apply to Pierre Wibaux, Royal Chambord ranch. Postoffice address, Mingusville, Dawson county, Dakota.

Pierre Wibaux.
articles.summary: Pierre Wibaux announces a winter bull ranch at the Royal Chambord ranch, $2 per bull per month.

From North Grand river, near stage station on November 3d, a light bay horse, five years old, about 16 hands high weighs about 1,300. Has a scar on the fleshy part of the left thigh, just below the tail, one white hind foot; on each front leg just above the fetlock joint has a small knot or splint, and shoulder badly galled with some white hairs on shoulder. Also a brown horse branded U S on left shoulder, I C on left side of hip and neck., is pigeon-toed in left fore foot. About ten years old weighs about 1,000 pounds. A reward of twenty dollars ($20) will be paid for information leading to their recovery.

Wm. Miller.
Minneseela, Butte Co., Dak.
articles.summary: Wm. Miller of Minnesela offers $20 for two horses strayed from North Grand river November 3.

articles.headline: NOTICE. Of a Proposed Meeting of the Stockmen of the Little Missouri.
articles.text:
At the request of Messrs. Huidekooper, Wadsworth, Eaton, Truscott, the N. P. R. C. Co. and of several other stockmen having ranges on the Little Missouri and Beaver Creek, a meeting of the stockmen of this river and its tributaries is hereby called to be held in Roberts Hall, Medora at 11 a. m. Friday December 19th. The object is to bring together the cattlemen of this vicinity in order that they may discuss certain questions of immediate and pressing interest to them, and in order that they may take measures to provide for a more efficient organization of the stockmen of this vicinity in the future, both so that they may be able to act more as a unit than has been the case in the past, and so that they can combine to protect their interests against unjust interference from the outside.

All gentlemen interested in stock raising both those on the Little Missouri, and those on the neighboring waters, are urgently requested to attend.

[By request.]

Theodore Roosevelt.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt's notice calling a meeting of Little Missouri stockmen at Roberts Hall, Medora, 11 a.m. Friday December 19.

articles.text: There is too much money invested in cattle in the United States for our friends to allow temporary differences of opinion of last. articles.headline: Advice?
articles.text:
The cattle owners in the Little Missouri country have wisely declined to have anything to do with a petition from that country to repeal the herd law for that section of the country. Such a repeal would work great injury to the settlement of the country, and it is good sense on the part of the stock owners to not interfere on this particular point, and it is further for their own interest to protect the settler from their herds, instead of the settler protecting himself. Fencing farm property belongs to a past age. Wise cattle owners will heed this, and as the advancing homesteader comes, they must and will protect him, that is men that have sense. A country that naturally feeds cattle, will when cultivated, raise all the cereals, roots, flax and vegetables. Cattlemen, be wise on this subject.—[Dakota Blade.

Uncle Jimmy Emmons often "flies open," but did it very effectually in the above article. There has never been started a petition for a repeal of the herd law here. Should there be one, it would receive the signature of every cattleman on the river. Such a repeal would not work injury to the settlement of this country, but help it, as the herd law is at present our greatest drawback. It is not for the interest of the cattle men to protect the settler as there is now, and from the nature of the Bad Lands always will be a thousand dollars invested in stock to one in agriculture. This country naturally feeds cattle, but except on the tops of high buttes and in places along the river is not at all adapted to agriculture. Jimmy, inform yourself on this subject.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy rebuts a Dakota Blade item by 'Uncle Jimmy' Emmons, saying no herd-law repeal petition has been started but every cattleman would sign one.

articles.headline: What's a Bronco.
articles.text: Pale, sedentary reader, who sittest in the calm seclusion of thy home and propoundest questions to the omniscient opinion-moulder, we will enlighten thy childish mind, and give you some pointers which we have been at great pains to gather. We use the word pains advisedly, and in its fullest sense. A bronco is a horse. He has four legs, like the saw-horse, but he is decidedly more skittish. The bronco is of gentle deportment and modest mien, but there isn't a real safe place about him. There is nothing mean about the bronco though, he is perfectly reasonable and acts on principle. All he asks is to be let alone, but he does ask this and even insists on it. He is firm in this matter and no kind of argument can shake his determination. There is a bronco that lives out some miles from this city. We know him right well. One day a man roped him and tried to put a saddle on him. The bronco looked sadly at him, shook his head and begged the fellow, as plain as could be, to go away and not try to interfere with a bronco who was simply engaged in the pursuit of his own happiness, but the man came on with the saddle and continued to aggress. Then the bronco reached out with his right hind foot and expostulated with him, so that he died. When thoroughly roused, the bronco is quite fatal, and if you can get close enough to him to examine his cranial structure, will find a cavity just above the eye where the bump of remorse should be. The bronco is what the cowboys call "high strung." If you want to know just how high he is strung, climb up on his apex. We didn't travel far, but the ride was mighty exhilarating while at lasted. We got on with great pomp and a derrick but we didn't put on any unnecessary style when we went to get off. The beast evinced considerable surprise when we took up our location upon his dorsal fin. He seemed to think a moment and then he gathered up his loins and delivered a volley of heels and hardware, a straight out from the shoulder. The recoil was fearful. We saw that our seat was going to be contested, and we began to make motions to dismount, but the beast had got under way by this time so we breathed a silent hymn and tightened our grip. He now went off into a spasm of tall stifflegged bucks. He pitched us up so high that, every time we started down, we would meet him coming up on another trip. Finally he gave us one grand, farewell boost and we clove the firmament and split up through the hushed ethereal until our toes ached from the lowness of the temperature, and we could distinctly hear the music of the spheres. Then we came down and fell, in a little heap about a hundred yards from the starting point. A kind Samaritan gathered up our remains in a cigar box and carried us to the hospital. As they looked pityingly at us, the attendent surgeons marveled as to the nature of our mishap. One said it was a cyclone, another that it was a railroad mash-up, but we thought of the calico-hide pony that was grazing peacefully in the dewy mead, and held our place.—[Santa Fe Democrat.
articles.summary: Humorous clipping from the Santa Fe Democrat describing a bronco ride.

articles.summary: Johnny Goodall has been breaking teams for the stage road.

articles.summary: James Hannigan and his wife plan to occupy one of the brick cottages.

articles.summary: Lumber has arrived for George Fitzgerald's new hotel.

articles.summary: George Gideon loaded his outfit Monday and pulled out with Roberts & Townsend's train.

articles.text: The dance at the Western house, Little Missouri, was well attended, and proved enjoyable to all participants.

articles.summary: Several more large cattle companies are expected to open ranches near Medora next spring.

articles.summary: Captain Wrenshall returned Tuesday evening to inspect the N. P. R. C. Co. slaughter house buildings.

articles.summary: The Christmas eve ball at Roberts & Co.'s hall is expected to surpass anything yet seen.

articles.summary: The season's last cattle shipment on the Northern Pacific will be three cars of SOHO company cattle to Jamestown.

articles.text: John O'Sullivan is going into winter quarters with vengeance. When he finishes his improvements, he will call his barber shop "The Gem."
articles.summary: John O'Sullivan is improving his barber shop, to be called "The Gem."

articles.summary: D. K. Wade graded a road from Tepee bottom onto the bench, avoiding the heavy sand road.

articles.text: Mrs. M. Liebmann, of Deadwood, came Monday night and was a guest at Rassie Deffebach's until yesterday morning, when she started for home on the coach.
articles.summary: Mrs. M. Liebmann of Deadwood visited Rassie Deffebach from Monday night until Wednesday morning.

articles.text: Some one is missing the opportunity of a lifetime in not establishing a harness and boot and shoe shop here. There is plenty of work to keep two men busy all winter.

articles.summary: H. M. Heath of Wells, Fargo & Co. was in Medora Tuesday making agent Maxwell agent for both express companies.

articles.text: Preparations are being made for the best ball Medora has ever seen, Christmas eve. It will be held in Roberts & Co.'s hall, under James Hannigan's management.
articles.summary: A Christmas eve ball is planned at Roberts & Co.'s hall under James Hannigan's management.

articles.text: Charles Cook is a good friend to the printer. He brought us over a pailfull of apple cider yesterday that was fit for the gods. He intends keeping it on sale for the future.
articles.summary: Charles Cook gave the printer apple cider and will keep it on sale.

articles.text: We have written a number of insurance policies during the last week, and hope soon to insure everything here. Every good business man wants his property insured.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office wrote a number of insurance policies during the week.

articles.text: Mr. and Mrs. Barr will start in a few days for St. Paul. From there Mrs. Barr will visit her relatives in Missouri, and Mr. Barr will go on to Fort Worth, Texas. They will return in the spring.
articles.summary: Mr. and Mrs. Barr will leave for St. Paul, Missouri and Fort Worth, returning in the spring.

articles.text: A visit to the Cow Boy office will convince anyone that there is no need of sending out of town for a wagon. We sell the celebrated Studebaker Bros.' make, and have prices down to bottom figures.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office sells Studebaker Bros. wagons.

articles.text: Joe Ferris had a naraow escape from a severe or fatal accident Tuesday morning. No. 2 barely slackened speed in Little Missouri, and Joe, in attempting to get on, was thrown violently to the ground, escaping with a few bruises.
articles.summary: Joe Ferris was thrown from the No. 2 train at Little Missouri Tuesday morning and escaped with bruises.

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt, who is taking an active interest in the coming cattle men's meeting, was in Medora Tuesday working up interest in that direction. When he knows he is right, Mr. Roosevelt's New York record shows that he is a tireless worker.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt was in Medora Tuesday drumming up interest in the coming cattlemen's meeting.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens will return in about ten days from Spearfish, where he is making preparations to move his family and effects to Medora, his future home. Until the Hotel de Mores is refitted he will live in one of the brick cottages.
articles.summary: Dr. H. M. Jorgens will return from Spearfish in about ten days to move his family to Medora.

articles.text: The season's killing at the slaughter house is ended, with the exception of the pigs. Every head of stock fit for slaughter will be killed, and an entirely new start made in the spring. It is the present intention to make a large drive from Texas, and to slaughter local cattle until they arrive. Meantime work is going on rapidly at the new slaughter house, and every preparation is being made for an opening on a large scale in the spring.
articles.summary: The slaughter house has ended the season's killing; a Texas drive and a large spring opening are planned.

Northern Pacific Railroad — "Going East or Going West"; St. Paul to Portland, Ore.; Chas. S. Fee, General Passenger Agent, St. Paul, Minn.
General Store of the N. P. R. C. Co., Medora, Dakota — groceries, dry goods, ready-made clothing, hats, caps, canned goods, harness, saddles, tobacco and cigars, felt shoes, overshoes, boots and shoes, flour and feed; hunters' outfits a specialty; wholesale and retail
Franz Falk Brewing Co., Milwaukee, Wis. — Milwaukee beer; agents Roberts & Co., Medora, Dak.; Otto Fisher, manager of Bismarck branch
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, fancy bits and spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores
Minneapolis & St. Louis R'y, "Famous Albert Lea Route" — S. F. Boyd, Gen'l Tkt. & Pass. Ag't, Minneapolis
Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, Dak. — wholesale dealers in wines, liquors, cigars; case and bar goods
Brand: Medora Stage & F. Co., A. T. Packard, General Manager, Medora, Dakota — horse brand on left shoulder; horses strung on stage stations between Medora and Deadwood; $25 reward
Brand: E. W. Casey & Co., Frank S. Moore, manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — KC (circle) on left hip and shoulder; range O'Donnell creek

Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, m'g'r, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — VI on left hip; range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river

Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota — E6 on left side; range Grand river; $100 reward re VVV or E6 ranges
Brand: H. R. Tarbell & Co., Medora, Dak. — horse brand on left shoulder; range Davis creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — TD on left hip
Brand: Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, manager, Medora — LC on left side; range Little Missouri south of the R. R.; ranch Tepee bottom; also owners of DW brand
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — SO on left side; range Little Missouri river and Beaver creek, north of N. P. R. R.
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora — several cattle brands on left side; also steers purchased of Mason & Lovell; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, manager, P.O. Medora — R (circle) on left hip; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora — circle-dot on cattle and horses; ranch/range north of crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri
Brand: Pennell & Roberts, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — RR and JP horse/mule brands; ranch four miles down river from crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — LSF on left shoulder; range O'Donnell creek
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., F. Alden Eaton, supt., P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — HK (circle) and other brands; range Little Missouri river, Deep and Davis[?] creeks
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — OX (approx.) on right side; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — 7L, bellows and Pd brands; range Little Missouri river fifteen miles north of Medora

articles.summary: Display advertisements and cattle and horse brand advertisements filling most of page 4.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt in Medora rallying support for the cattlemen's meeting
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt, taking an active interest in the coming cattlemen's meeting, was in Medora on Tuesday working up interest in it. The paper noted his New York record as a tireless worker.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt, who is taking an active interest in the coming cattle men's meeting, was in Medora Tuesday working up interest in that direction.

events.date_basis: Stated: "Friday December 19th" (1884)
events.title: Roosevelt calls a meeting of Little Missouri stockmen for December 19
events.summary: A notice signed by Theodore Roosevelt, at the request of Huidekooper, Wadsworth, Eaton, Truscott, the N. P. R. C. Co. and other stockmen, called a meeting of stockmen of the Little Missouri and its tributaries at Roberts Hall, Medora, at 11 a.m. Friday, December 19, to organize and protect their interests.
events.excerpt: a meeting of the stockmen of this river and its tributaries is hereby called to be held in Roberts Hall, Medora at 11 a. m. Friday December 19th.

events.date_basis: Stated: "meeting of December 19"
events.title: Cow Boy urges full attendance at the stockmen's meeting
events.summary: The Cow Boy, printing the meeting notice for the second time, urged every cattleman in the district to attend the December 19 meeting so that an organization could be formed.
events.excerpt: A number of points will come up for action at the meeting of December 19, and it is important that every cattle man in this district attend

events.date_basis: "Saturday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Marquis de Mores leaves for Chicago
events.summary: The Marquis de Mores went to Chicago on Saturday and was expected back on Monday.
events.excerpt: Marquis de Mores went to Chicago Saturday. He will be back Monday.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday morning" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Joe Ferris thrown from train at Little Missouri
events.summary: Joe Ferris narrowly escaped serious injury Tuesday morning when the No. 2 train barely slowed at Little Missouri and he was thrown to the ground trying to board; he escaped with bruises.
events.excerpt: No. 2 barely slackened speed in Little Missouri, and Joe, in attempting to get on, was thrown violently to the ground, escaping with a few bruises.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday evening" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: J. C. Fisher returns from Deadwood
events.summary: J. C. Fisher returned from Deadwood on Tuesday evening.
events.excerpt: J. C. Fisher returned from Deadwood Tuesday evening.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: C. W. Sleeper on trip to Helena
events.summary: C. W. Sleeper was on an extended trip to Helena and western points.
events.excerpt: C. W. Sleeper is on an extended trip to Helena and western points.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Roberts & Co. buy a burglar- and fire-proof safe
events.summary: Roberts & Co. acquired a first-rate burglar and fire proof safe.
events.excerpt: Roberts & Co. have indulged in a first-rate burglar and fire proof safe.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Roller rink busy in Medora
events.summary: The roller skaters at the rink were limited only by the number of skates.
events.excerpt: The roller skaters at the rink are only limited by the number of skates.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Johnny Goodall breaks teams for the stage road
events.summary: Johnny Goodall had been breaking several teams for use on the stage road.
events.excerpt: Johnny Goodall has been breaking several teams for use on the stage road.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Work to begin on George Fitzgerald's new hotel
events.summary: Lumber arrived and work was soon to begin in earnest on George Fitzgerald's new hotel.
events.excerpt: Lumber has arrived and work will soon begin in earnest on George Fitzgerald's new hotel.

events.date_basis: "last Monday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: George Gideon pulls out with Roberts & Townsend's freight train
events.summary: George Gideon loaded his outfit Monday and pulled out with Roberts & Townsend's outfits.
events.excerpt: George Gideon loaded his outfit last Monday, and pulled with Roberts & Townsend's.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Roberts & Townsend freight outfits leave for the Black Hills
events.summary: Roberts & Townsend's outfits loaded with 40,000 pounds of Black Hills freight pulled out on Tuesday.
events.excerpt: Roberts & Townsend's outfits loaded with 40,000 pounds of Hills freight and pulled out Tuesday.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Dance at the Western House, Little Missouri
events.summary: A dance at the Western House in Little Missouri was well attended and enjoyed by all.
events.excerpt: The dance at the Western house, Little Missouri, was well attended, and proved enjoyable to all participants.

events.date_basis: "next spring" after Dec 1884
events.title: More cattle companies expected near Medora
events.summary: The paper was assured that several more large cattle companies intended to open ranches near Medora the next spring.
events.excerpt: several more large cattle companies intend opening ranches near Medora next spring.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday evening" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Captain Wrenshall inspects the N. P. R. C. Co. slaughter house
events.summary: Captain Wrenshall returned Tuesday evening to again inspect the N. P. R. C. Co.'s slaughter house buildings.
events.excerpt: Captain Wrenshall returned Tuesday evening to again inspect the N. P. R. C. Co.'s slaughter house buildings here.

events.date_basis: "Christmas eve" 1884
events.title: Christmas eve ball planned at Roberts & Co.'s hall
events.summary: A Christmas eve ball was being prepared at Roberts & Co.'s hall under James Hannigan's management, billed as the best ball Medora had seen.
events.excerpt: Preparations are being made for the best ball Medora has ever seen, Christmas eve. It will be held in Roberts & Co.'s hall, under James Hannigan's management.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue; shipment upcoming
events.title: Season's last cattle shipment: SOHO cattle to Jamestown
events.summary: The last cattle shipment of the season on the Northern Pacific was to be three car loads of the SOHO cattle company's cattle to Jamestown.
events.excerpt: The last shipment of cattle on the N. P. R. R. for the season will be three car loads of the SOHO cattle company's to Jamestown.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: John O'Sullivan improves barber shop, "The Gem"
events.summary: John O'Sullivan was improving his barber shop for winter and planned to call it "The Gem."
events.excerpt: When he finishes his improvements, he will call his barber shop "The Gem."

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: D. K. Wade grades road at Tepee bottom
events.summary: D. K. Wade graded a road onto the bench south of Tepee bottom, avoiding the heavy sand road.
events.excerpt: D. K. Wade has made a great improvement in Tepee bottom by grading a road onto the bench south of the bottom

events.date_basis: "Monday night" to "yesterday morning" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Mrs. M. Liebmann of Deadwood visits Medora
events.summary: Mrs. M. Liebmann of Deadwood arrived Monday night and stayed with Rassie Deffebach until Wednesday morning, when she left for home on the coach.
events.excerpt: Mrs. M. Liebmann, of Deadwood, came Monday night and was a guest at Rassie Deffebach's until yesterday morning, when she started for home on the coach.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Wells, Fargo & Co. express opens at Medora with agent Maxwell
events.summary: H. M. Heath of Wells, Fargo & Co.'s express was in Medora Tuesday, making agent Maxwell agent for two rival express companies.
events.excerpt: H. M. Heath, of Wells, Fargo & Co.'s express, was here Tuesday, initiating agent Maxwell into the double-headed act of being agent for two rival express companies.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Cow Boy editorial attacks Northern Pacific rates
events.summary: In "A Kick," the Cow Boy welcomed Wells, Fargo express competition and complained that freight to Medora cost more than freight shipped on to Deadwood, and that N. P. passenger and telegraph rates were extortionate.
events.excerpt: it shows that there is "something rotten in Denmark."

events.date_basis: "yesterday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Charles Cook brings cider to the Cow Boy
events.summary: Charles Cook brought the printer a pailful of apple cider and planned to keep it on sale.
events.excerpt: He brought us over a pailfull of apple cider yesterday that was fit for the gods.

events.date_basis: "during the last week" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Cow Boy office writes insurance policies
events.summary: The Cow Boy wrote a number of insurance policies during the week.
events.excerpt: We have written a number of insurance policies during the last week

events.date_basis: "in a few days" after Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Mr. and Mrs. Barr to leave for the winter
events.summary: Mr. and Mrs. Barr planned to leave in a few days for St. Paul; Mrs. Barr would visit Missouri and Mr. Barr Fort Worth, returning in spring.
events.excerpt: Mr. and Mrs. Barr will start in a few days for St. Paul.

events.date_basis: "in about ten days" after Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Dr. H. M. Jorgens to move his family to Medora
events.summary: Dr. H. M. Jorgens was expected back in about ten days from Spearfish, where he was preparing to move his family to Medora, living in a brick cottage until the Hotel de Mores was refitted.
events.excerpt: Dr. H. M. Jorgens will return in about ten days from Spearfish, where he is making preparations to move his family and effects to Medora, his future home.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Slaughter house ends season's killing
events.summary: The season's killing at the slaughter house ended except for the pigs; plans called for a large drive from Texas and a large-scale opening of the new slaughter house in spring.
events.excerpt: It is the present intention to make a large drive from Texas, and to slaughter local cattle until they arrive.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 11 Dec 1884
events.title: Cow Boy job press breaks
events.summary: The Cow Boy's job press suffered a severe break Tuesday; George Wilkes was to repair it.
events.excerpt: Our job press sustained a severe break Tuesday, but George Wilkes will soon set it going.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Old telegraph office stuck on a flat car
events.summary: The old telegraph office building was still on a flat car across the river, too broad to pass the bridges west, and would be sold in Medora.
events.excerpt: The old telegraph office is still loaded on a flat car across the river.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Gill Kennedy paints the company's offices
events.summary: Gill Kennedy was improving the company's offices with a coat of paint.
events.excerpt: Gill Kennedy is improving the company's offices with a coat of paint.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Magpies plague hunters' meat down the river
events.summary: Hunters down the river had trouble keeping magpies from pecking at their meat.
events.excerpt: The hunters down the river find considerable difficulty in preserving their meat from the attacks of magpies

events.date_basis: "the coming meeting" = stockmen's meeting Fri 19 Dec 1884
events.title: Citizens ask cattlemen to honor school fund pledge
events.summary: Several citizens wrote that the cattlemen had promised to subscribe to the school fund and hoped it would be taken up at the coming meeting.
events.excerpt: The cattle men promised to subscribe to our school fund, and we hope the matter will be taken up at the coming meeting.

events.date_basis: Stated: "January 1" (1885)
events.title: Territorial legislature to convene at the new Bismarck capitol
events.summary: The legislature was to convene at the new capitol in Bismarck on January 1; E. W. Martin, newly elected, was urged by Black Hills papers for speaker.
events.excerpt: E. W. Martin, recently elected legislator, is urged especially by the Black Hills papers for speaker.

events.date_basis: Stated: "October 5" (1884)
events.title: Medora stage company horse strays
events.summary: The M. S. & F. Co. offered $25 for a sorrel horse with four white feet that strayed on October 5.
events.excerpt: From M. S. & F. Co., October 5, one sorrel horse; four white feet, white stripe in face

events.date_basis: No date given; notice in Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: W. N. Thompson & Co. horse lost from round-up
events.summary: W. N. Thompson & Co. offered $10 for a bay horse lost from the Little Missouri round-up.
events.excerpt: Lost from the Little Missouri round-up, one bay horse 5 years old

events.date_basis: Stated: "the night of November 19" (1884)
events.title: Mare strayed or stolen from A. Young's ranch
events.summary: A. Young reported a dark sorrel mare strayed or stolen from his ranch ten miles south of Medora on the night of November 19.
events.excerpt: From my ranch on Little Missouri, ten miles south of Medora, the night of November 19, a dark sorrel mare

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Cattle outfits offer $250 reward against grass fires
events.summary: Seven outfits, including the N. P. Ref. Car Co., Continental Cattle Co. and E. G. Paddock, offered $250 for information leading to the arrest of anyone setting grass fires in western Dakota's cattle sections.
events.excerpt: The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Gregor Lang offers reward for missing horses
events.summary: Gregor Lang offered $50 for the return of three mares and a sorrel pony.
events.excerpt: The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock

events.date_basis: Stated: "Monday, November 18th, 1884" (Nov 18, 1884 fell on a Tuesday; printed date used)
events.title: Pierre Wibaux starts bull round-up for winter bull ranch
events.summary: Pierre Wibaux announced a bull ranch on the Little Missouri at the Royal Chambord ranch, caring for bulls over winter at $2 a month; the bull round-up started November 18.
events.excerpt: The bull round-up started on Monday, November 18th, 1884, and all bulls will be received at the Royal Chambord ranch.

events.date_basis: Stated: "November 3d" (1884)
events.title: Two horses stray from North Grand river
events.summary: Wm. Miller of Minnesela offered $20 for two horses that strayed from near the North Grand river stage station on November 3.
events.excerpt: From North Grand river, near stage station on November 3d, a light bay horse

events.date_basis: Stated: "December 4" (1884)
events.title: Frank Walker takes up two stray ponies
events.summary: Frank Walker took up two stray ponies at the Knutson creek sheep corral on December 4.
events.excerpt: Had halter on when taken up, December 4.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 11 Dec 1884 issue
events.title: Cow Boy disputes herd-law item from Dakota Blade
events.summary: Answering a Dakota Blade item, the Cow Boy said no petition to repeal the herd law had been started on the Little Missouri, but that every cattleman would sign one, calling the herd law the country's greatest drawback.
events.excerpt: There has never been started a petition for a repeal of the herd law here. Should there be one, it would receive the signature of every cattleman on the river.
